facts.statement: Bungartius was an extinct joint-necked fish that lived in Ohio during the Late Devonian period.
facts.quote: Bungartius is an extinct genus of arthrodire ("joint-necked") fish from the Late Devonian period of Ohio.

facts.statement: Bungartius is the only known member of its family, Bungartiidae, and is related to the giant fish Titanichthys.
facts.quote: It is the sole member of the family Bungartiidae, related to the giant Titanichthys.

facts.statement: The first specimen of Bungartius was found by Peter A. Bungart in Cuyahuga County, Ohio, within the Cleveland Shale Member of the Ohio Shale.
facts.quote: The first specimen of Bungartius was recovered by Peter A. Bungart in Cuyahuga County, Ohio, and came from strata belonging to the Cleveland Shale Member of the Ohio Shale.

facts.statement: In 1936, Peter Anthony Bungart recovered a concretion containing dorsal and ventral armor plates from Cuyahuga County, Ohio.
facts.quote: In 1936, Peter Anthony Bungart, a staff member of the Cleveland Museum of Natural History, recovered a concretion containing the dorsal and ventral armour plates of an unknown fish from Cuyahoga County, Ohio, by Peter A. Bungart.

facts.statement: David H. Dunkle formally described the genus and species Bungartius perissus in 1947.
facts.quote: In 1947, Dunkle described the two specimens and erected a new taxon, Bungartius perissus.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Bungartius may have been a durophage, feeding on hard-shelled invertebrates.
facts.quote: Bungartius may have been durophagous, meaning that it would have eaten hard-shelled invertebrates.

facts.statement: Bungartius was a mid-sized arthrodire with a cranial shield length of 40.5 cm.
facts.quote: Bungartius was a mid-sized arthrodire, with a total cranial shield length, measured from the rostral tip to the hind margin of the paranuchal bones (analogous to the tabular bones of modern bony fishes), of 40.5 cm.

facts.statement: The lower jaw plates of Bungartius were large, lacked cusps, and ended in a short, downward-inclined tip.
facts.quote: The inferognathal plates, those of the lower jaw, are non-cuspidate (lacking cusps), and were quite large, terminating in a short, downward-inclined extremity.

facts.statement: Thickened shearing surfaces on the lower jaw suggest Bungartius was adapted for crushing hard prey.
facts.quote: The inferognathal plates' symphyseal regions bore thickened occlusal surfaces that were ideally suited as shearing surfaces, and it has been suggested as a result that Bungartius was durophagous.

facts.statement: The dorsal body armor of Bungartius was short, low, and narrow, similar to its skull.
facts.quote: The dorsal (upper) body armour is fairly short, though is low and narrow, like the skull.

facts.statement: The spinal plates in front of the pectoral fin attachment were completely atrophied, and the postero-lateral plates have not yet been identified.
facts.quote: The spinal plates, which sit in front of the pectoral fenestra (where the pectoral fin attaches) are completely atrophied, and, as of yet, the postero-laterals have not been identified.

facts.statement: In 1975, Robert Howland Denison classified Bungartius into its own family, Bungartiidae.
facts.quote: In 1975, Robert Howland Denison assigned Bungartius to a family of its own, Bungartiidae.

facts.statement: Robert Howland Denison suggested that the family Bungartiidae belonged to the clade Pachyosteina, which included dominant placoderms of the Upper Devonian.
facts.quote: He suggested that the family belonged to Pachyosteina, a paraphyletic placoderm clade that represented the "dominant placoderms of the Upper Devonian".

facts.statement: A 2017 phylogenetic analysis placed Bungartius as an intermediate form between Tafilalichthys and Titanichthys.
facts.quote: In a 2017 phylogenetic analysis, Bungartius was placed as an intermediate between Tafilalichthys and Titanichthys.

facts.statement: Bungartius lived during the Famennian stage, between 365.2 and 358.86 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Famennian to Famennian (365.2 to 358.86 million years ago)

rejected.statement: A second, more complete specimen was discovered in 1943 by David H. Dunkle, who formally named the genus and species in 1947.
rejected.quote: A second, more complete specimen was discovered in 1943 by David H. Dunkle, who, four years later, named a new genus and species to accommodate them.

rejected.statement: In 1943, David H. Dunkle recovered an almost complete specimen that was approximately twice the size of the earlier find.
rejected.quote: In 1943, palaeontologist David H. Dunkle recovered an almost complete specimen (CMNH 7573), which was around twice as large as that recovered by Bungart.

rejected.statement: It is currently unclear whether Bungartius possessed a Meckelian groove, though it may have been absent.
rejected.quote: It is not clear whether Bungartius had a Meckelian groove, though it may have been absent.
